title: Songbird Jet Ltd., Inc. v. Amax Inc.
lead: Negotiations over a corporate jet produced competing accounts of a finished sale, while separate brokerage, fraud, and restitution theories failed on summary judgment.

actors.name: Songbird Jet and Jet Leasing
actors.role: Aircraft firms pursuing a resale transaction

proceedings: Amax sought summary judgment dismissing plaintiffs’ four theories.
District court left the sales-contract claim for trial and dismissed brokerage, fraud, and unjust enrichment.
limits: The negotiations and deposit purpose remained disputed. No finding established a sale, executive authority, or accepted part payment. Amax counterclaims remained unresolved; separate retained-deposit claims had been settled.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: Amax reduces its fleet amid financial losses
sections.cue: The parties describe different versions of a multiaircraft arrangement
paragraphs: In 1982 mineral-and-energy company Amax sought to reduce its corporate fleet: two operating Falcons, a jet leased from plaintiffs, and an undelivered Falcon 50, serial 108, under construction. It assigned financing manager David Ayres, administrative vice president Edward Miller, and flight manager Jack Esposito to the task. Songbird Jet and Jet Leasing bought, sold, brokered, and serviced aircraft through principals Alan Rosefielde, a former tax lawyer, and William Handy, a former airline pilot.

Plaintiffs described a June arrangement to find a buyer for 108 and earn the purchase-resale spread. Amax instead described an inseparable package: 108 for $9.4 million, another jet for $7.5 million, a leaseback of plaintiffs’ plane, and cancellation of an existing lease. A July 1 board resolution authorized an agreement or agreements. Amax said lower offers and disposition of the leaseback plane repudiated the package; plaintiffs claimed a separate sale later formed.

sections.title: A proposed resale shapes the autumn negotiations
sections.cue: Unsigned drafts and a retained deposit point in different directions
paragraphs: By September plaintiffs found Texas oil businessman L.R. French, who wanted to trade a Lear jet and did not need tax benefits. Rosefielde proposed buying 108, reselling it to French with the trade, and letting Amax sell tax benefits separately. The plan required service before January 1983. He said Ayres obtained senior approval and announced a deal about October 28 for $8,850,000, down from roughly $9 million for modifications, with a $250,000 price deposit and an acceptable French contract.

Plaintiffs supplied first an unsigned then French-signed agreement and tendered the deposit. Its letter made the money refundable on request and creditable if an agreement was finalized. Amax viewed it as consideration to remove the jet from the market; plaintiffs said part payment. Ayres allegedly demanded changed payees and immediate payment or the deal was off. Amax endorsed the final check and held it over two months.

Lawyers produced drafts in November and early December, but neither party signed the sale. Plaintiffs regarded papers as memorialization and sent personnel to monitor completion at AiResearch for year-end delivery and tax treatment. On December 22 Amax denied a contract and withdrew the plane. It sold tax benefits December 29 and returned the deposit January 3, retaining $53,789.68 as a disputed debt. Separate claims over that retention later settled by consent order. Plaintiffs sued in January 1983.

sections.title: Summary judgment cannot resolve authority or contractual intent
sections.cue: The writing defense fails only if the deposit was accepted as payment
paragraphs: Plaintiffs asserted sales breach, a separate brokerage contract, a knowingly insincere promise, and unjust enrichment for negotiation, tax structuring, and monitoring. Amax counterclaimed and sought summary judgment on plaintiffs’ theories. Applying undisputed New York law, Judge Edward Weinfeld drew reasonable inferences against Amax without deciding contested testimony.

The board’s reference to agreement or agreements did not conclusively require one inseparable package. Executive responsibilities, prior dealings, and a directive permitting 10% price adjustments could support implied or apparent authority, while other evidence could show authority only to submit offers for approval. Likewise, refundable language and unsigned drafts favored Amax without conclusively disproving present assent; parties may condition obligation on execution or merely anticipate a later memorial.

The Uniform Commercial Code writing requirement was not otherwise satisfied. Amax’s counterclaim admitted a package, not this separate sale, and the board resolution, ratification memorandum, French agreement, and unsigned drafts lacked a sufficient Amax-signed writing establishing the alleged relationship. Oral proof could not supply it.

But § 2-201(3)(c) allowed enforcement for goods with payment made and accepted. Accepted part payment for an indivisible jet could support the whole sale. The large deposit supported plaintiffs, yet Amax’s off-market explanation remained possible under New York’s unequivocally-referable requirement. Its purpose and acceptance needed trial, so the sales claim survived without a formation ruling.

sections.title: The remaining theories cannot turn negotiations into compensation
sections.cue: The court separates failed proof from categorical legal bars
paragraphs: The alleged brokerage arrangement was instead a purchase for plaintiffs’ own resale. They set French’s price, bore resale risk, and would owe Amax even if the resale failed. Board authorization and knowledge of that business model did not separately hire brokers.

New York could recognize fraud in a promise made with undisclosed present intent not to perform, but evidence was missing. Rosefielde’s belief that Amax’s chief executive wanted the plane for personal or family use was unsupported; continued conferences and drafts contradicted a sham. An unexplained diary entry did not establish intent.

Unjust enrichment required benefit and injustice, not merely plaintiffs’ unrecovered deal expenses. Finding French, negotiating resale, and sharing information pursued their own advantage. The tax idea was publicly known to Amax and the industry and contemplated by Treasury regulations, not a novel contribution. Monitoring was closer because plaintiffs might think a sale already existed, but it still protected their resale and year-end price structure. Amax disputed any benefit and had an independent December-delivery entitlement. Even incidental benefit from voluntary self-interested services did not justify restitution here.

sections.title: Only the sales theory proceeds
sections.cue: The motion does not resolve Amax’s counterclaims
paragraphs: Weinfeld denied summary judgment on the sales-contract claim and granted it on the other claims, directing an implementing order within five days on at least three days’ notice. No damages or sale finding followed, and Amax’s counterclaims were not adjudicated. The outcome left the disputed bargain alive while rejecting the attempts to recover the same failed-transaction efforts through brokerage, fraud, or unjust enrichment.
